name: Elena Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we do not sell anything or campaign. What you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Elena Okafor, 43, and I do junior carpentry and general work on building sites. I live with my partner and our two school-age children; the mortgage is a regular worry, but I like seeing a wall straight after a day of work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you do from the time you arrive until you finish for the day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I help unload boards, mark lengths, carry offcuts and hold frames while the experienced carpenter fixes them. I am still learning, and I prefer someone to show me a task once instead of handing me another screen to figure out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a little help with the delivery list is fine if it gets the right boards to site. I would still want the carpenter to look at them before anyone cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of the work I do is carrying, holding and fitting, so I do not expect a small office change to remove my tasks. My worry is the pay because there is less than a month of savings if the site closes for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep accepting the shifts I already get and ask the supervisor before the weekend about the next week. If work is short, I would wait to replace household things that are still usable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The change sounds small for the work I do with my hands. I still feel tense when I think about one missed week taking away money we need for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before cutting a new delivery of boards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the length with the opening and ask the carpenter if something looks off. I still need someone to check that timber fits the room before I cut it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household expense would be hardest to postpone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children need their usual school things, and I would not want to delay those. We could wait on replacing a chair or other household item that still works.

say: I would say **a clear delivery list** helps if it brings the right boards to site.
I would still want **the carpenter to check** before anyone cuts.
think: I do not expect a **small office change** to remove my carrying and fitting tasks.
I have **thin savings**, so a week without work would hurt.
do: Keep accepting the **shifts I get** and ask before the weekend about next week.
Wait to replace **usable household items** if work is short.
feel: **The change feels small**, but a missed week could take money needed for the mortgage.
S0.quote: I still need someone to check that timber fits the room before I cut it.
fieldNote: She sees little direct impact on her **hands-on tasks** in this mild scenario.
**Thin savings** make a single week without work a real household worry.

steps.text: Keep accepting current shifts and ask about next week before the weekend
Delay replacing household items that still work if site pay is short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say I am slow with new screens, but I can learn a site task if someone stands with me. I would rather try a real delivery list than pretend I understand a tool I have not used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may use AI to plan deliveries or write site notes, and I do not know how many of those tasks I will still be asked to help with. I can learn after I see the tool used, but I cannot afford unpaid classes or months between jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor to show me one screen task while I am on shift, then repeat it with the next delivery. I would keep doing the carrying and fitting work I already know while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cautious because I do not like learning from a screen without anyone beside me. I would try if the lesson happened during paid work and did not ask me to buy a new device.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a new tool easier for you to trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to compare its list with the paper plan and the actual room. If it is wrong, I need to know whom to tell before material is wasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you do if the supervisor did not have time to teach it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a coworker to show me when the site was quiet, but I would not pretend I had it right before someone checked. If nobody can help, I would keep to the tasks I already do safely.

say: I am **slow with new screens**, but I can learn a site task with someone beside me.
I would rather try a **real delivery list** than pretend I understand an unused tool.
think: I think the office may use AI for delivery plans and **site notes**, and I do not know which tasks will remain.
I can learn after seeing a tool, but I cannot afford **unpaid classes** or months between jobs.
do: Ask the supervisor to show me **one screen task** during a shift and practise on the next delivery.
Keep doing the **carrying and fitting** I already know while I learn.
feel: I feel **cautious** about screens without help, but I would try paid instruction on the current device.
S1.quote: I am slow with new screens, but I can learn a site task if someone stands with me.
fieldNote: She resists learning alone but is open to a **supervised work task**.
**Unpaid training** or buying a device would conflict with the household budget.
**Few local jobs** limit alternatives if her hours fall.

steps.text: Learn one AI screen task from the supervisor during a paid shift
Keep doing current carrying and fitting tasks while learning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the thinking part changes first, before robots are ready to work on a site. I would not promise anyone that using our hands keeps us employed until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could take measurements, notes and schedules that I sometimes help with, so I would lose that part of my work in 2028. There may be practical tasks left for a while, but I cannot count a robot delay as three years of certain wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028, I would ask the carpenter to show me how to fit a door frame and check it square. In 2029, I would ask what shifts are actually available and keep money for the mortgage before buying tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is not much time to become good at a job I am still learning. I would try to learn the practical work, but I cannot promise that it will be enough to keep my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children if your hours were reduced in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would explain that we may have to postpone a family outing and be careful about extra spending. I would reassure them that they did nothing wrong, while being honest that work might be uneven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you think about the three years before robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use that time to learn practical tasks if the site still has work and someone can teach me. I would not assume a job exists just because the robots come later.

say: I would say **thinking tasks change first**, before robots work on a site.
I would not promise **hands-on work** keeps us employed until 2031.
think: I think AI could take **measurements, notes and schedules** that I sometimes help with in 2028.
I cannot count a **robot delay** as three years of certain wages.
do: Ask the carpenter to teach me to **fit a door frame** before 2028.
In 2029, ask about **available shifts** and keep mortgage money before buying tools.
feel: **Two years** is little time to become good at a job I am still learning.
I would practise, but cannot promise it will protect **my pay**.
S2.quote: I cannot count a robot delay as three years of certain wages.
fieldNote: She understands the difference between **thinking tasks in 2028** and robots later.
Her 2029 plans depend on **available shifts** and a worker willing to teach her.

steps.text: Learn fitting door frames from an experienced carpenter before 2028
In 2029, protect mortgage money before buying tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives a little more time to learn than two years. I would also say the time only helps if a site gives junior workers real practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031, AI could do the notes and measurements I sometimes help with. Robots arriving around 2034 could affect the carrying and fitting too, so I would not call my current trade safe for the whole period.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for one new practical task each year and let the carpenter check my work. In 2032, I would look for actual hiring information before spending on a course or leaving my current line of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me room to practise without rushing into a decision. I still feel anxious because our savings would not cover many weeks if the site stopped giving me shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which practical task would you try first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would choose one door frame and ask the carpenter to check its level before I fix it. I would rather learn one cut properly than promise a certificate will find me a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What information would you want before considering a different job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a local builder what tasks they hire for and how many shifts they can offer. If the answer is uncertain, I would not leave a job I already have for a rumor.

say: I would say **five years** gives a little more time to learn than two years.
I would also say the time only helps if sites provide **real practice** for junior workers.
think: I think AI could do **site notes** that I sometimes help with by 2031.
I would not call my current trade **safe through 2034**, when robots could affect physical tasks.
do: Ask for **one new practical task** each year and have the carpenter check my work.
In 2032, check **actual hiring information** before paying for a course or leaving my field.
feel: **Five years gives room** to practise without rushing a decision.
I still feel anxious because our **savings** would not cover many weeks without shifts.
S3.quote: I would rather learn one cut properly than promise a certificate will find me a job.
fieldNote: She turns the longer warning into **supervised practice**, without treating it as a job guarantee.
**Actual hiring information** would be needed before she risks leaving her current work.

steps.text: Ask for another practical task each year and get the work checked
In 2032, check local hiring before deciding whether to leave the field

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years gives people a chance to see changes coming and make decisions as they learn. I would not say construction is safe just because the robots arrive later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect AI could do the work notes and planning by 2036, and robots could reach physical jobs around 2039. My children will be older, and their choices may change what our household needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep learning practical carpentry while a site can offer me paid practice. In 2037, my partner and I would talk with the children about the older one’s studies when the choices are close, not decide now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives me time to watch which tasks are still being hired for. I still worry because the mortgage is due each month, and nobody knows whether I can keep working after the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change what the children study now because of this card?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not choose a path for them while they are still at school. We can listen to what they want and look at the choices that exist when the time comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years let you do that two years did not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could practise across several years and find out what site employers still need. The extra time would help me make better choices, but it would not pay next month’s mortgage for me.

say: I would say **ten years gives time** to see changes and make choices as I learn.
I would not call **construction safe** just because robots arrive later.
think: I expect AI could do **work notes and planning** by 2036, with robots reaching physical jobs around 2039.
**My children** will be older, and their choices may change what our household needs.
do: Keep learning **practical carpentry** while paid practice is available.
In 2037, discuss **the older child’s studies** with my partner and children when choices are close.
feel: A **decade gives time** to see which site tasks are still hired.
I still worry about **the mortgage** due each month and whether work will last after the robot date.
S4.quote: My children will be older, and their choices may change what our household needs.
fieldNote: She values a **longer warning** but does not assume construction stays secure.
**Family needs may shift** as her children grow and make study choices.
She cannot assume current **school costs** will stay the same as the children grow.

steps.text: Keep learning practical carpentry while sites offer paid practice

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I have little time to learn or build savings. A patient supervisor can teach me more than a new screen can, and steady shifts would help us keep the mortgage current.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I am not against every new tool, but I need to see how it works on the real job and have someone check me. A patient supervisor can teach me more than a new screen can.

headlineQuote: A patient supervisor can teach me more than a new screen can.
portrait: Elena is a **junior worker** supporting her partner and two school-age children.
Her **thin savings** make missed site shifts difficult to absorb.
She prefers **hands-on teaching** and is slow to take up unfamiliar technology.
She sees **robot risk** as later, not a guarantee of secure work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives her little time to learn or build savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Patient supervision** and steady shifts would help her keep the mortgage current.
